Author(s):

Himantveer Kaur, Muskan Kohli, Ansh Bindal, Arnav Chandla

SkinSense is an AI-based skin analysis and skincare recommendation app. It predicts skin type and acne severity from a user-submitted photo, then generates a personalised skincare routine and product recommendations -- filtered by budget, allergies, and ingredient conflicts -- with weekly longitudinal tracking and a dermatologist-referral safety net for severe or low-confidence cases.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Week 11 : Alembic Migration Running on Wrong Database
Alembic Running on SQLite Instead of PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Error: 

INFO  [alembic.runtime.migration] Running upgrade  -> a1b2c3d4, add skin_type_source column
sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError: (sqlite3.OperationalError) near "ALTER": syntax error
[SQL: ALTER TABLE analysis_results ADD COLUMN skin_type_source VARCHAR]

Relevant Context The DATABASE_URL environment variable had been set using setx in a previous terminal session:

setx DATABASE_URL "postgresql+psycopg2://postgres:password@localhost:5432/skinsense"

Then Alembic was run in what appeared to be a new terminal:

alembic upgrade head

Key Observation setx writes the variable to the Windows registry for future processes. It does not affect the terminal that ran it, nor any process already open — including VS Code and all terminals inside it. So Alembic was still picking up the SQLite URL from the VS Code session that was open before setx was called.

Solution Use set (not setx) in the same terminal where Alembic will run:

set DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg2://postgres:password@localhost:5432/skinsense
alembic upgrade head

Because set writes to the current process's environment immediately. setx writes to the registry and only takes effect for processes started after that point. VS Code and its integrated terminals inherit the environment that VS Code itself was started with, so setx changes are invisible until VS Code is restarted.

docs.title: Duplicate Column Error on Re-Run
docs.text:
Error: 

sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError: (sqlite3.OperationalError) duplicate column name: skin_type_source

Relevant Context Even after opening a new VS Code integrated terminal, the error persisted. The migration had appeared to succeed once, then ran again on the same SQLite file:

alembic upgrade head
# ran on SQLite, appeared to succeed
# opened new terminal, ran again
alembic upgrade head
# duplicate column error — column already existed on SQLite

Key Observation VS Code's integrated terminal inherits the environment that VS Code was launched with. Opening a new terminal tab inside VS Code does not pick up setx changes — only fully restarting VS Code does. The migration was still running against the SQLite file on both attempts.

Solution Close VS Code completely and reopen it. The new VS Code process inherits the registry value set by setx, so all integrated terminals inside it will now have the correct DATABASE_URL.

# After restarting VS Code
echo %DATABASE_URL%
# should print: postgresql+psycopg2://postgres:password@localhost:5432/skinsense
alembic upgrade head
# now runs against PostgreSQL

Because Windows environment inheritance works at process creation time. Each process gets a copy of its parent's environment. VS Code's terminal spawns from VS Code's own environment, not from the registry. A full VS Code restart creates a new process that reads the registry values set by setx.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This week I fixed the Alembic migration setup so it reliably runs against PostgreSQL. The root cause was a Windows environment variable inheritance issue: setx does not update running processes. The fix is either to use set for the current terminal session or to restart VS Code fully after setx. The database migration for the skin_type_source column then ran cleanly against PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Week 12 : ResNet-50 Checkpoint Key Mismatch and Frontend 409 Handling
ResNet-50 State Dict Key Mismatch on Load
docs.text:
Error: 

RuntimeError: Error(s) in loading state_dict for ResNet:
        Unexpected key(s) in state_dict: "model.conv1.weight", "model.bn1.weight",
        "model.bn1.bias", "model.layer1.0.conv1.weight" ...
        Missing key(s) in state_dict: "conv1.weight", "bn1.weight" ...

Relevant Context The checkpoint was saved from a training wrapper class that wrapped the ResNet inside a self.model attribute:

# training script — how the checkpoint was saved
class AcneClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = resnet50(pretrained=True)
        self.model.fc = nn.Linear(2048, 3)

trainer = AcneClassifier()
torch.save(trainer.state_dict(), "resnet50_acne.pt")
# keys saved as: "model.conv1.weight", "model.layer1.0.conv1.weight" ...

But at inference time the checkpoint was loaded directly into a bare ResNet:

# inference.py — original broken load
model = resnet50(pretrained=False)
model.fc = nn.Linear(2048, 3)
model.load_state_dict(torch.load("resnet50_acne.pt"))
# bare ResNet keys: "conv1.weight", "layer1.0.conv1.weight" ...
# mismatch with the "model." prefix in the checkpoint

Key Observation The checkpoint keys carry a model. prefix from the wrapper class. The inference-time model has no wrapper, so its keys have no prefix. PyTorch's load_state_dict does an exact string match on keys — any prefix difference causes a full failure.

Solution Strip the model. prefix from every key before loading:

import collections

raw = torch.load("resnet50_acne.pt", map_location="cpu")
fixed = collections.OrderedDict(
    (k[len("model."):] if k.startswith("model.") else k, v)
    for k, v in raw.items()
)
model = resnet50(pretrained=False)
model.fc = nn.Linear(2048, 3)
model.load_state_dict(fixed)
model.eval()

Because torch.save(module.state_dict()) serialises the keys exactly as they appear in the module hierarchy. Wrapping a model in self.model prepends model. to every key. Stripping the prefix at load time realigns the keys without needing to re-export the checkpoint.

docs.title: Frontend Not Handling HTTP 409 from Predict Endpoint
docs.text:
Error: No crash in the backend. But after uploading a photo without first saving a skin type, the frontend displayed a generic error message instead of prompting the user to enter their skin type.

Relevant Context The predict endpoint returns 409 when skin type has not been recorded and the user has not filled in the profile:

# inference.py — backend 409 response
if not user.skin_type and not body.skin_type:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="skin_type_required")

The original frontend fetch just caught all non-2xx responses as a generic error:

// Upload.jsx — original
const res = await fetch("/api/predict", { method: "POST", body: formData });
if (!res.ok) {
  setError("Something went wrong. Please try again.");
  return;
}

Key Observation A 409 from this endpoint has a specific meaning: the backend needs skin type to be provided before it can run inference. That is not the same as a generic failure and needs its own UI path.

Solution Check for 409 specifically and return a sentinel that the calling component can act on:

// Upload.jsx — fixed
const res = await fetch("/api/predict", { method: "POST", body: formData });
if (res.status === 409) {
  return { skinTypeRequired: true };
}
if (!res.ok) {
  setError("Something went wrong. Please try again.");
  return;
}
const data = await res.json();

Because HTTP status codes carry semantic meaning. A 409 Conflict here signals a specific precondition failure, not a server error. Handling it separately lets the UI show a targeted prompt instead of a generic error that leaves the user unsure what went wrong.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This week I integrated the trained ResNet-50 acne severity model into the backend. The main blocker was a state dict key mismatch caused by the training checkpoint being saved from a wrapper class. Stripping the key prefix at load time fixed it without re-training. I also improved the frontend to handle the 409 response from the predict endpoint so users are properly directed to fill in their skin type before running analysis.

docs.title: Week 14 : Seed Script UniqueViolation and Feedback Router Not Registered
UniqueViolation on Seed Re-Run
docs.text:
Error: 

psycopg2.errors.UniqueViolation: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "analysis_results_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (id)=(1) already exists.
sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError: (psycopg2.errors.UniqueViolation) ...
ROLLBACK

Relevant Context The seed script tried to clear and re-insert demo progress rows in a single transaction:

# seed.py — original broken version
def seed_demo_progress(db: Session):
    db.execute(text("DELETE FROM analysis_results WHERE user_id IN (1, 2, 3)"))
    for row in DEMO_ROWS:
        db.add(AnalysisResult(**row))
    db.commit()   # DELETE and INSERT in the same transaction

Key Observation When PostgreSQL hits the UniqueViolation on the INSERT it aborts the entire transaction, including the DELETE that already ran. The DELETE and INSERT were both in the same transaction, so they rolled back together and the original rows were still there.

Solution Commit the DELETE in its own transaction before inserting:

# seed.py — fixed version
def seed_demo_progress(db: Session):
    db.execute(text("DELETE FROM analysis_results WHERE user_id IN (1, 2, 3)"))
    db.commit()   # commit the DELETE first
    for row in DEMO_ROWS:
        db.add(AnalysisResult(**row))
    db.commit()   # then commit the INSERTs

Because PostgreSQL aborts the entire transaction on any error, including constraint violations. By committing the DELETE separately, the rows are gone before the INSERT tries to add them again, so there is nothing to conflict with.

docs.title: Feedback Endpoint Returning 404
docs.text:
Error: 

404 Not Found
{"detail": "Not Found"}

Posting to /api/feedback returned 404 even though feedback.py existed and had the router defined correctly.

Relevant Context The feedback router was defined and working in isolation but was never added to the main app:

# feedback.py — router was correct
router = APIRouter()

@router.post("/feedback")
async def submit_feedback(...):
    ...

# main.py — original, missing the feedback router
from fastapi import FastAPI
from . import auth, inference, recommendations, progress, health

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(auth.router, prefix="/api")
app.include_router(inference.router, prefix="/api")
app.include_router(recommendations.router, prefix="/api")
app.include_router(progress.router, prefix="/api")
app.include_router(health.router)
# feedback.router never registered

Key Observation FastAPI only routes requests to routers that have been explicitly registered with app.include_router(). Defining a router in a module does not register it.

Solution Import and register the feedback router in main.py:

# main.py — fixed
from . import auth, inference, recommendations, progress, health, feedback

app.include_router(feedback.router, prefix="/api")

Because FastAPI builds its route table at startup from the routers that are explicitly included. A router that is not passed to include_router is simply ignored, which is why the endpoint returned 404 instead of 405 or 500.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This week I completed the demo seed data setup and wired up the feedback endpoint. The seed fix required understanding how PostgreSQL transaction semantics differ from SQLite — a constraint violation aborts the whole transaction, not just the failing statement. The feedback 404 was a straightforward omission: the router had not been registered in main.py.

docs.title: Week 15 : Test KeyError After API Refactor and bcrypt Compatibility Break
KeyError in Progress Test After Response Shape Changed
docs.text:
Error: 

FAILED tests/test_analysis.py::test_progress_returns_results - KeyError: 'results'

Relevant Context The progress endpoint had been refactored to return a bare list instead of a wrapped object, but the test still expected the old shape:

# Old endpoint response shape
{"results": [...], "count": 3}

# New endpoint response shape (after refactor)
[
  {"id": 1, "acne_severity": "mild", ...},
  {"id": 2, "acne_severity": "moderate", ...}
]

# test_analysis.py — original test, written against the old shape
def test_progress_returns_results(client, auth_headers):
    res = client.get("/api/progress", headers=auth_headers)
    assert res.status_code == 200
    data = res.json()
    assert len(data["results"]) > 0   # KeyError: 'results' — data is now a list

Key Observation The endpoint contract changed during refactoring but the tests were not updated. The test assumed a dict with a "results" key, but the endpoint now returns a plain JSON array.

Solution Update the test to match the new response shape:

# test_analysis.py — fixed
def test_progress_returns_results(client, auth_headers):
    res = client.get("/api/progress", headers=auth_headers)
    assert res.status_code == 200
    data = res.json()
    assert isinstance(data, list)
    assert len(data) > 0

Because When an API response shape changes, every test that inspects the response body needs to be updated to match. The fix is to assert the new shape directly, using isinstance(data, list) to confirm it is no longer a dict.

docs.title: passlib AttributeError with bcrypt 4.1
docs.text:
Error: 

AttributeError: module 'bcrypt' has no attribute '__about__'

Raised on every password hash or verify call, breaking login and registration completely.

Relevant Context The error appeared after pip install -r requirements.txt on a fresh environment. requirements.txt had no pin on bcrypt:

# requirements.txt — original
passlib[bcrypt]==1.7.4
# bcrypt version unpinned — pip installs latest (4.1 at the time)

passlib 1.7.4 reads the bcrypt version at import time like this:

# passlib internals — why it breaks
import bcrypt
version = bcrypt.__about__.__version__   # AttributeError: bcrypt has no attribute '__about__'

bcrypt 4.1 removed __about__ and switched to importlib.metadata for version introspection.

Key Observation passlib 1.7.4 has not been updated to handle bcrypt 4.x. The __about__ attribute it reads was removed in bcrypt 4.1.

Solution Pin bcrypt to 4.0.1, the last version that still has __about__:

# requirements.txt — fixed
passlib[bcrypt]==1.7.4
bcrypt==4.0.1

Because passlib 1.7.4 is essentially unmaintained. Pinning bcrypt to 4.0.1 keeps passlib working without changing the auth code. The underlying hashing is still secure — the break was only in version introspection.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This week I ran the full test suite and fixed the two failures. The first was a stale test that had not been updated after the progress endpoint response shape changed. The second was a dependency incompatibility between passlib and bcrypt that breaks all password operations on fresh installs. Both are now fixed and all tests pass.

docs.title: Week 16 : Alembic DuplicateColumn After Manual DDL and JWT Refresh 422 on Missing Key
DuplicateColumn Error from Manual ALTER TABLE
docs.text:
Error: 

sqlalchemy.exc.ProgrammingError: (psycopg2.errors.DuplicateColumn)
column "skin_concern" of relation "user_profiles" already exists

Relevant Context The skin_concern column had been added to the table manually using psql while Alembic was not being used:

-- ran directly in psql
ALTER TABLE user_profiles ADD COLUMN skin_concern VARCHAR;

Later, an Alembic migration was written to add the same column:

# migrations/versions/xxxx_add_skin_concern.py
def upgrade():
    op.add_column("user_profiles", sa.Column("skin_concern", sa.String(), nullable=True))

When alembic upgrade head ran, it tried to add a column that already existed in PostgreSQL, causing the error.

Key Observation Alembic tracks which migrations have run in its alembic_version table, not what columns actually exist in the database. The manual ALTER TABLE created the column in the database but Alembic did not know about it, so it tried to add it again.

Solution Tell Alembic to treat the migration as already applied without running it:

alembic stamp xxxx_add_skin_concern

Or, if you want future robustness, use IF NOT EXISTS in the migration:

def upgrade():
    op.execute("ALTER TABLE user_profiles ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS skin_concern VARCHAR")

Because alembic stamp updates the alembic_version table to mark a revision as applied without executing the migration SQL. This re-syncs Alembic's view of the world with what actually exists in the database.

docs.title: JWT Refresh Endpoint Returns 422 When Body Key Is Wrong
docs.text:
Error: 

POST /api/auth/refresh  →  422 Unprocessable Entity
{
  "detail": [
    {
      "loc": ["body", "refresh_token"],
      "msg": "field required",
      "type": "value_error.missing"
    }
  ]
}

Relevant Context The frontend was sending the refresh call with the key token instead of refresh_token:

// auth.js — before fix
const response = await api.post("/api/auth/refresh", {
  token: localStorage.getItem("refresh_token"),   // wrong key
});

The FastAPI endpoint expected:

# auth.py
class RefreshRequest(BaseModel):
    refresh_token: str

@router.post("/auth/refresh")
def refresh(payload: RefreshRequest, session: Session = Depends(get_session)):
    ...

Pydantic validated the body against RefreshRequest and rejected the request because the refresh_token field was absent. The error appeared only after JWT expiry, so it was not caught during earlier testing when access tokens were still valid.

Key Observation Pydantic model field names must match exactly what the client sends. A wrong key name does not raise a 400 — it raises 422 with a Pydantic validation error listing the missing field. The bug was invisible during initial testing because access tokens had a one-hour TTL and tests did not wait for expiry.

Solution Match the request body key to the Pydantic model field:

// auth.js — after fix
const response = await api.post("/api/auth/refresh", {
  refresh_token: localStorage.getItem("refresh_token"),  // correct key
});

Because FastAPI uses Pydantic to parse and validate JSON request bodies. If a required field is missing from the JSON object, Pydantic raises a ValidationError and FastAPI returns 422 automatically before the route function runs. Renaming the client-side key to match the model field resolves the mismatch.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This week I fixed two issues that surfaced during final integration. The first was an Alembic state mismatch caused by a manual DDL change — resolved by using alembic stamp to sync the migration history with the actual database schema. The second was a 422 error on the JWT refresh endpoint caused by the frontend sending the wrong JSON key — resolved by correcting the key name to match the Pydantic model field. Both issues were only visible in a fully integrated environment, not in isolated unit tests.

docs.title: Use-Case Modelling
docs.text:
I worked on the SkinSense use-case diagram. The main actors were defined as User and Admin.

For the User, I mapped the analysis flow from Upload Selfie for Analysis to Verify Face Photo, Predict Skin Type, Predict Acne Severity, and View Analysis Results. The recommendation-related functions were separated into Get Product Recommendations, Check Ingredient Conflicts, View Recommendation Explanation, Set Price Preference, Build AM/PM Routine, and View Safety Disclaimer.

For the Admin, I added Manage Product & Ingredient Database to represent maintenance of the product and ingredient information used by the recommendation engine.

Track Skin Progress was kept as a planned future feature because periodic tracking is not part of the current core implementation.

docs.title: Technical Review
docs.text: I checked the relationships between the use cases so that prediction functions support the analysis result and recommendation functions operate after analysis. PostgreSQL was not added as an actor because it is an internal database component.

docs.title: Reference Study
docs.text:
I reviewed the ACNE04 method used for the planned acne-severity model. The referenced preprocessing uses three severity classes: mild (1-5), moderate (6-20), and severe (>20). The method also applies class balancing, resizing, and normalization before model training.

No application code was written during this task.

docs.title: Backend Schemas and Storage
docs.text: I set up the request/response schemas for the upload and predict endpoints, along with the local storage handling for uploaded images. This gave the rest of the backend a fixed shape to build against before any real model logic existed.

docs.title: /api/upload and /api/predict
docs.text: I implemented /api/upload and /api/predict with stub inference wired in, plus the referral-flag logic (returning a placeholder "see a dermatologist" flag for now). The stub returns a deterministic response so the frontend team could build against a stable contract while the real ResNet-50 model was still in training.

docs.title: Integrating Ansh's Recommendation Router
docs.text: Once Ansh's stub recommendation engine and router were ready, I wired his router into main.py so the full request chain (upload → predict → recommend) worked end to end through one FastAPI app.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
I ran the backend and frontend together locally and walked through the full flow: uploading a photo, getting a stub severity/skin-type prediction, and receiving a stub product list with an AM/PM routine. This became the definition-of-done check for the week: a clean clone had to run both servers and complete the flow, including the manual-fallback path if a model step failed.

No trained models were involved yet; this week was purely about getting the skeleton running.

docs.title: Week 6 : Data Pipelines and First Training Run
ACNE04 Preprocessing
docs.text:
I preprocessed the ACNE04 dataset following the approach in the reference paper (Zhang and Ma). The steps were:

  • Relabelled the lesion counts into three severity classes: mild (1-5), moderate (6-20) and severe (>20).
  • Built the train/test split from the paper's fold 0 instead of a random split, so our numbers stay comparable to the paper.
  • Resized all images to 224x224 and normalized them with the ImageNet mean and std, since ResNet-50 starts from ImageNet weights.
  • Applied class-count smoothing, because the severe class has far fewer images than mild and moderate.
  • Checked the raw annotation format against the paper's description before running the relabelling script.
  • Checked that images from the same patient or session do not end up on both sides of the split. The 99%+ accuracy in the paper is most likely inflated by this kind of leakage, and we would rather report a lower number that holds up.

docs.title: Skin-Type Data Preparation
docs.text: With Muskan, I worked on the data side of the skin-type notebook. We finished collecting the dry class (about 250 images, with a source log) and cleaned the oily and normal classes taken from Kaggle by removing duplicates and fixing labels.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The ACNE04 split and the smoothing weights are what the first ResNet-50 run trains on. If the run's numbers look wrong, those are the first two things to check.

docs.title: PostgreSQL and Migrations
docs.text: Until this week the app was only really running on SQLite, even though Postgres was the plan. I set up PostgreSQL locally and added Alembic for migrations, so schema changes can be applied without editing the database by hand.

docs.title: AnalysisResult Model
docs.text: I added an AnalysisResult model and table to store each user's predictions (severity, skin type, confidence and timestamp). It is not connected to /api/predict yet, so for now the endpoint returns a prediction without saving it.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text: /api/predict and /api/recommendations are now behind JWT auth, and /api/ingredients stays public. Refresh tokens use token versioning so they can be revoked on logout. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt. I pinned bcrypt==4.0.1 because passlib==1.7.4 breaks on newer bcrypt versions.

docs.title: Real Acne Inference
docs.text:
I replaced the stub with the trained ResNet-50 checkpoint (resnet50_acne.pt). Loading it with the standard torchvision constructor failed with mismatched keys, because the checkpoint was saved from a feature-wrapped version of the model. I changed the loader to detect which format the checkpoint uses and build the matching model. The API now returns source: "model" for real predictions. The stub can still be used with the SKINSENSE_USE_REAL_MODELS flag.

There is no skin-type model yet, so /api/predict with a photo now needs a skin_type in the request. The backend uses that value with a confidence of 1.0.

docs.title: Product Catalog
docs.text: I built the product catalog from kingabzpro/cosmetics-datasets. The raw file had 1,472 rows and 1,325 were left after removing junk entries from the scrape. The ingredient reference list now has 25 ingredients, our original 12 plus 13 taken from the amaboh dataset. The seeded catalog has 1,333 products: the 1,325 real ones and 8 hand-written toner and serum entries, so those routine steps always have something to show.

docs.title: Merging Branches
docs.text: I merged Muskan's frontend branch into mine. The only conflict was in inference.py, where her branch still had the old stub version. I kept the real inference version.

docs.title: Tests

docs.title: Week 8 : MediaPipe Photo Validation and Predict Endpoint Wiring
Photo Validation Crashing on JPEG Upload
docs.text:
Error: 

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../photo_validation.py", line 34, in validate_photo
    results = face_detection.process(image_array)
ValueError: data type must be uint8
  (MediaPipe received a 1-D buffer of compressed bytes instead of a decoded image)

Relevant Context The validation gate was receiving the raw uploaded file bytes from FastAPI and passing them straight to MediaPipe:

# photo_validation.py — original broken version
async def validate_photo(file: UploadFile) -> ValidationResult:
    contents = await file.read()
    image_array = np.frombuffer(contents, dtype=np.uint8)
    with mp_face_detection.FaceDetection(min_detection_confidence=0.5) as face_detection:
        results = face_detection.process(image_array)

Key Observation np.frombuffer on JPEG bytes produces a 1-D array of compressed data. MediaPipe's .process() needs a decoded H x W x 3 RGB numpy array. The raw bytes are still JPEG-compressed, not pixel data.

Solution Decode the image with PIL first, convert to RGB, then hand it to MediaPipe:

# photo_validation.py — fixed version
from PIL import Image
import io

async def validate_photo(file: UploadFile) -> ValidationResult:
    contents = await file.read()
    pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(contents)).convert("RGB")
    image_array = np.array(pil_image, dtype=np.uint8)   # H x W x 3, uint8
    with mp_face_detection.FaceDetection(min_detection_confidence=0.5) as face_detection:
        results = face_detection.process(image_array)

Because MediaPipe's Python bindings call into native C++ code that expects a contiguous uint8 array shaped (H, W, 3). PIL's .open().convert("RGB") fully decodes the JPEG and produces exactly that shape and dtype.

docs.title: AnalysisResult Not Being Saved After Prediction
docs.text:
Error: No crash. The /api/predict endpoint returned results but nothing appeared in the analysis_results table. Queries to /api/progress returned an empty list every time.

Relevant Context The predict endpoint was calling the ML model and returning the JSON response, but the SQLAlchemy insert was missing:

# inference.py — predict endpoint, original
@router.post("/predict")
async def predict(file: UploadFile, db: Session = Depends(get_db), user = Depends(get_current_user)):
    validation = await validate_photo(file)
    result = run_inference(file)
    return result   # never saved to DB

Key Observation The endpoint returned the model output correctly but never committed an AnalysisResult row. All progress tracking and history depend on that row existing.

Solution Insert the row before returning:

@router.post("/predict")
async def predict(file: UploadFile, db: Session = Depends(get_db), user = Depends(get_current_user)):
    validation = await validate_photo(file)
    result = run_inference(file)
    db_result = AnalysisResult(
        user_id=user.id,
        acne_severity=result["acne_severity"],
        skin_type=result["skin_type"],
        skin_type_source=result.get("skin_type_source", "manual"),
        confidence_acne=result["confidence"]["acne"],
        confidence_skin_type=result["confidence"]["skin_type"],
        referral_needed=result["referral_needed"],
    )
    db.add(db_result)
    db.commit()
    return result

Because SQLAlchemy does not auto-persist objects. db.add() stages the row in the session and db.commit() flushes it to PostgreSQL. Without that the ORM object only exists in memory for the duration of the request.

docs.title: Week 11 : Referral Flag Not Triggering for Low Confidence and Inconsistent Return Type
Referral Flag Not Triggering for Low-Confidence Predictions
docs.text:
Error: No crash. Users with low-confidence skin type or acne predictions were not being shown the referral recommendation, even though the design required it.

Relevant Context The referral check only looked at acne severity, not confidence scores:

# recommendations.py — original broken version
def should_refer(result: AnalysisResult) -> bool:
    if result.acne_severity == "severe":
        return True
    return False

Key Observation A prediction can have moderate acne severity but very low confidence — meaning the model was not sure of its result. That is exactly when a referral is most useful. Checking only severity missed all the low-confidence cases.

Solution Add confidence thresholds as additional referral conditions:

# recommendations.py — fixed version
CONF_THRESHOLD = 0.60

def should_refer(result: AnalysisResult) -> bool:
    if result.acne_severity == "severe":
        return True
    if result.confidence_acne < CONF_THRESHOLD:
        return True
    if result.confidence_skin_type < CONF_THRESHOLD:
        return True
    return False

Because Low model confidence is a signal that the prediction may be unreliable, regardless of the predicted severity class. A dermatologist referral is appropriate whenever the app cannot give a confident answer.

docs.title: get_recommendations Returning dict in One Path and list in Another
docs.text:
Error: 

TypeError: object of type 'dict' has no len()
  File "recommendations.py", line 112, in get_recommendations
    if len(recs) == 0:

Relevant Context get_recommendations had two return paths that returned different types:

# recommendations.py — original inconsistent return
def get_recommendations(profile: UserProfile, result: AnalysisResult):
    if result.skin_type is None:
        return {"error": "skin_type_required", "recommendations": []}
    # ... normal path ...
    return [Product(...), Product(...), ...]
    # one path returns dict, the other returns list

The router called len(recs) on the return value, which works for a list but raises TypeError on a dict.

Key Observation The early-return path was returning a dict with error metadata while the normal path returned a list of products. The router did not check which type it received before calling len().

Solution Standardise the return type to always be a list, and handle the error condition in the router:

# recommendations.py — fixed, always returns list
def get_recommendations(profile: UserProfile, result: AnalysisResult) -> list:
    if result.skin_type is None:
        return []

    recs = build_recommendations(profile, result)
    return recs

# router — handle the empty list case
@router.get("/recommendations")
async def recommendations(user = Depends(get_current_user), db = Depends(get_db)):
    result = get_latest_result(db, user.id)
    if result is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="no_analysis_found")
    if result.skin_type is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="skin_type_required")
    recs = get_recommendations(user.profile, result)
    return recs

Because A function should return a consistent type. Mixing dict and list in return paths forces every caller to check the type before using the return value. Moving the error signalling to HTTP exceptions in the router keeps the business logic function simple and type-consistent.

docs.title: Week 12 : Recommendations Engine Returning Wrong Shape and Budget Filter Currency Mismatch
get_recommendations Returns Dict Instead of List for Products
docs.text:
Error: 

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
  at Recommendations.jsx:48

Relevant Context The frontend called result.products.map(...) but products was a plain object, not an array. The engine was returning a dict keyed by product id:

# recommendations/engine.py — before fix
def get_recommendations(session, skin_type, acne_severity, ...):
    ...
    products = {}
    for candidate in kept:
        products[candidate.id] = {
            "id": candidate.id,
            "name": candidate.name,
            ...
        }
    return {
        "products": products,   # dict, not list
        "routine": routine,
        ...
    }

The React component expected an array:

// Recommendations.jsx
{result.products.map((p) => (     // TypeError — .map is not a function on {}
  <ProductCard key={p.id} product={p} />
))}

Key Observation Python dicts and JavaScript objects look similar but React array methods (map, filter, length) only work on actual arrays. Returning products as a dict broke every component that iterated over it. The API contract between backend and frontend must be agreed on a list type for collections.

Solution Return products as a list in the engine:

# recommendations/engine.py — after fix
    products = []
    for candidate in kept:
        products.append({
            "id": candidate.id,
            "name": candidate.name,
            ...
        })
    return {
        "products": products,   # list — .map works in React
        "routine": routine,
        ...
    }

Because JSON arrays map to JavaScript arrays, which have .map(). JSON objects map to plain JavaScript objects, which do not. The fix aligns the return type with what the Pydantic response model (RecommendationResponse) and the frontend both expect.

docs.title: Budget Filter Comparing INR Prices Against USD Ceiling
docs.text:
Error: No crash. But products priced at ₹400–₹600 were being excluded when the user set a budget of 500. The user expected ₹500 to include ₹400 products — but the filter was treating prices as USD.

Relevant Context Product prices in products.json were stored in INR (e.g. "price": 450). The budget ceiling coming in from the frontend was also in INR. But an earlier version of the seed script had stored prices in USD and multiplied by USD_TO_INR = 83.5 only for display. After the seed was updated to store native INR prices, the display conversion was removed — but the budget comparison was never updated. It was still comparing raw stored values as if they were USD:

# rules.py — before fix (prices stored as INR, budget in INR)
def budget_filter(candidates, budget_max):
    if budget_max is None:
        return candidates, []
    kept, dropped = [], []
    for c in candidates:
        # c.price is ₹450, budget_max is ₹500
        # comparison is correct numerically, but old code had a
        # USD_TO_INR conversion here that was left in by mistake:
        price_in_comparison_units = c.price * 83.5   # ← bug: double-converting
        if price_in_comparison_units > budget_max:
            dropped.append(Excluded(c.id, c.name, f"₹{c.price} is above your ₹{budget_max} per-product budget."))
        else:
            kept.append(c)
    return kept, dropped

A ₹450 product was being compared as 450 × 83.5 = 37,575 against a budget of 500, so it was always excluded.

Key Observation When the seed script was refactored to store prices natively in INR, the stale USD_TO_INR multiplier in budget_filter was not removed. This made the budget filter reject almost every product regardless of the user's ceiling.

Solution Remove the stale conversion — compare price directly in INR:

# rules.py — after fix
def budget_filter(candidates, budget_max):
    if budget_max is None:
        return candidates, []
    kept, dropped = [], []
    for c in candidates:
        if c.price > budget_max:   # both in INR — no conversion needed
            dropped.append(Excluded(c.id, c.name, f"₹{c.price} is above your ₹{budget_max} per-product budget."))
        else:
            kept.append(c)
    return kept, dropped

Because Once prices are stored in a single currency throughout the pipeline, no conversion is needed at comparison time. The bug survived refactoring because the multiplier was embedded in the filter logic rather than in the seed script where the currency decision was made.

docs.title: Week 14 : Budget Filter USD vs INR Mismatch and AM Routine Step Order
Budget Filter Rejecting Products Due to Currency Mismatch
docs.text:
Error: No crash. With a budget of 500 INR set in the profile, the recommendations endpoint returned an empty list even for products that cost less than 500 INR.

Relevant Context The products in the database had prices in USD from the original CSV. The user's budget was stored in INR. The filter compared them directly:

# recommendations.py — original broken filter
def filter_by_budget(products: list, budget_max: float) -> list:
    return [p for p in products if p.price <= budget_max]

# Example:
# p.price = 6.00  (USD — Cetaphil cleanser)
# budget_max = 500  (INR)
# 6.00 <= 500 is True — but 6 USD is ~501 INR, so should be excluded
# A product at p.price = 2.50 USD = 209 INR — should pass, does pass
# A product at p.price = 8.00 USD = 668 INR — should fail, passes (8 <= 500)

The comparison was numerically working in some cases but logically wrong throughout.

Key Observation Prices were in USD but the user's budget was in INR. Direct comparison of USD values against an INR budget gives wrong results for most products.

Solution Convert all product prices to INR at seed time, store INR in the database:

# seed.py — fixed price conversion
USD_TO_INR = 83.5

for _, row in df.iterrows():
    price_inr = round(float(row["price_usd"]) * USD_TO_INR, 2)
    db.add(Product(
        name=row["name"],
        price=price_inr,   # stored in INR
        ...
    ))

Because Storing prices in a single currency avoids per-query conversion and prevents currency mismatch bugs. INR is the right choice since the target users are in India and the budget input is in INR.

docs.title: AM Routine Putting SPF Before Moisturiser
docs.text:
Error: No crash. The generated AM routine was ordering steps as: cleanser, serum, SPF, moisturiser — SPF was placed before moisturiser, which is the wrong application order.

Relevant Context The routine builder sorted products alphabetically within each step category:

# routine.py — original broken sort
def build_am_routine(products: list) -> list:
    return sorted(products, key=lambda p: p.category)
# alphabetical: cleanser < moisturiser < serum < spf
# but correct order is: cleanser > toner > serum > moisturiser > spf

Alphabetical sorting gives moisturiser before spf correctly by coincidence, but serum comes before moisturiser alphabetically, which is wrong.

Key Observation Skincare application order is not alphabetical. The correct order is defined by product absorption: thinnest consistency first, thickest last, with SPF always last in the AM routine.

Solution Define an explicit step order and sort by index:

# routine.py — fixed version
AM_STEPS = ["cleanser", "toner", "serum", "eye_cream", "moisturiser", "spf"]

def build_am_routine(products: list) -> list:
    def step_index(product):
        try:
            return AM_STEPS.index(product.category)
        except ValueError:
            return len(AM_STEPS)   # unknown categories go last
    return sorted(products, key=step_index)

Because Explicit ordering by list index enforces the correct clinical application sequence. Unknown categories are placed at the end rather than causing a crash or sorting incorrectly.

docs.title: Week 15 : Skin Type Widening Too Narrow and README Missing Model Download Step
Skin Type Fallback Widening Only for "normal"
docs.text:
Error: No crash. Users with skin type "dry" or "oily" were getting fewer recommendations than expected. The minimum product count check was failing for them even though there were enough products in the catalog.

Relevant Context The recommendation engine had a fallback that widened the skin type pool when too few results were found:

# recommendations.py — original broken widening
def get_recommendations(profile, result):
    recs = query_products(skin_type=result.skin_type, budget=profile.budget_max)

    if len(recs) < MIN_RECS:
        # only widened for "normal" — dry and oily never widened
        if result.skin_type == "normal":
            recs += query_products(skin_type="combination", budget=profile.budget_max)

    return recs[:MAX_RECS]

Key Observation The widening was written only for "normal" skin type. Users with "dry" or "oily" skin type hit the low-count branch but got no widening, so they still received fewer recommendations than the minimum.

Solution Define explicit widening groups for all three skin types:

# recommendations.py — fixed version
SKIN_TYPE_WIDENING = {
    "dry":    ["dry", "normal"],
    "normal": ["normal", "dry", "oily"],
    "oily":   ["oily", "normal"],
}

def get_recommendations(profile, result):
    recs = query_products(skin_type=result.skin_type, budget=profile.budget_max)

    if len(recs) < MIN_RECS:
        wider = SKIN_TYPE_WIDENING.get(result.skin_type, [result.skin_type])
        recs = query_products(skin_types=wider, budget=profile.budget_max)

    return recs[:MAX_RECS]

Because The widening dict makes the fallback explicit and symmetric for all skin types. dry widens to include normal products (which are generally safe for dry skin), oily widens to include normal, and normal can use products from all three categories.

docs.title: Week 16 : Test Suite Failing on Routine ID Consistency and Conflict Filter Missing Forced-Time Assignment
test_routine_ids_all_appear_in_products Fails When max_products Truncates After Routine Is Built
docs.text:
Error: 

FAILED tests/test_recommendations.py::test_routine_ids_all_appear_in_products
AssertionError: assert 'prod_spf50' in {'prod_niacinamide', 'prod_salicylic', 'prod_ceramide'}

Relevant Context The test checks that every product id in routine["am"] and routine["pm"] also appears in products:

# test_recommendations.py
def test_routine_ids_all_appear_in_products(session):
    result = get_recommendations(session, skin_type="oily", acne_severity="moderate")
    product_ids = {p["id"] for p in result["products"]}
    for pid in result["routine"]["am"] + result["routine"]["pm"]:
        assert pid in product_ids   # ← AssertionError

The engine was building the routine from the full filtered candidate list, then slicing products down to max_products afterward:

# engine.py — before fix
kept, excluded = apply_all_filters(candidates, ...)
routine = build_routine(kept)          # built from all kept candidates
products = [format(c) for c in kept][:max_products]   # truncated after
return {"products": products, "routine": routine, ...}

Products that did not make the max_products cut still appeared in the routine because the routine was built from the untruncated list.

Key Observation The routine must be derived from the same final products list that is returned, not from the full pre-truncation list. If truncation happens after routine building, the routine references product ids that the client will never receive.

Solution Truncate kept before passing it to build_routine:

# engine.py — after fix
kept, excluded = apply_all_filters(candidates, ...)
kept = kept[:max_products]            # truncate first
routine = build_routine(kept)         # routine only references kept ids
products = [format(c) for c in kept]
return {"products": products, "routine": routine, ...}

Because The products list and the routine lists must reference the same set of candidate ids. Building the routine before truncation breaks this invariant and causes the client to receive a routine that references ids it cannot display.

docs.title: Conflict Filter Leaves lower.forced_time as None When Both Products Are step_time="both"
docs.text:
Error: No crash. But test_conflicting_pair_never_lands_in_the_same_routine_half was failing intermittently:

FAILED tests/test_recommendations.py::test_conflicting_pair_never_lands_in_the_same_routine_half
AssertionError: assert not ({'retinol', 'salicylic acid'} <= kept_ingredients_by_slot['pm'])

Relevant Context Both retinol and salicylic acid products had step_time="both" in the catalog. The conflict_filter "separate" rule was supposed to assign the higher-ranked one to AM and the lower-ranked one to PM. But the assignment for the lower product only ran if lower.forced_time is None and lower.step_time == "both":

# rules.py — before fix
if row["severity"] == "separate":
    higher_slot = higher.forced_time or (higher.step_time if higher.step_time != "both" else None)
    ...
    if higher_slot is None:
        higher.forced_time = "am"
    if lower.forced_time is None and lower.step_time == "both":
        lower.forced_time = "pm" if higher.forced_time == "am" or higher_slot == "am" else "am"

When higher.step_time == "both" and higher.forced_time was None before the block ran, higher_slot evaluated to None. The condition higher_slot is None fired and set higher.forced_time = "am" — but the lower.forced_time assignment checked higher.forced_time == "am" or higher_slot == "am". At that point higher_slot was still None (computed before the assignment), so the condition used the freshly-set higher.forced_time == "am" correctly. However, on a second pass through the loop the same products were processed again and higher.forced_time was already "am", so higher_slot was now "am" — but lower.forced_time had already been set, so the branch was skipped. The logic was correct for the first pair but left lower.forced_time as None when the conflict row appeared more than once (duplicate entries in the conflict table).

Key Observation Duplicate rows in the ingredient conflict table caused the same product pair to be processed twice. On the second pass, lower.forced_time was already set so the assignment branch was skipped — but this was fine. The real bug was that higher_slot was computed at the top of the block before higher.forced_time could be assigned, so when higher.step_time == "both" the slot was None and the assignment guard if higher_slot is None was used to set it, working correctly for a single pass. The intermittent test failure came from catalog data where duplicated conflict rows triggered additional iterations after the forced times were already set, occasionally resetting state.

Solution Compute higher_slot after the forced-time assignment, and guard against reprocessing a pair whose slots are already set:

# rules.py — after fix
if row["severity"] == "separate":
    if higher.forced_time is None and higher.step_time == "both":
        higher.forced_time = "am"
    higher_slot = higher.forced_time or higher.step_time

    if lower.forced_time is None and lower.step_time == "both":
        lower.forced_time = "pm" if higher_slot == "am" else "am"
    elif lower.forced_time is None:
        lower_slot = lower.step_time
        if higher_slot and lower_slot and higher_slot == lower_slot:
            dropped_ids.add(lower.id)
            dropped.append(Excluded(lower.id, lower.name, row["reason"] + " (could not be scheduled apart)"))

Because Computing a slot variable before the assignment that sets it and then checking the variable for None as the trigger for that same assignment creates an ordering dependency. Separating the assignment from the slot read makes the control flow explicit and removes the dependence on iteration order. Deduplicating conflict table lookups at query time also prevents double-processing.

docs.title: Week 8 : Conflict Rule Blocking Valid AM/PM Split Routines and Catalog Junk Entries
Conflict Rule Blocking Benzoyl Peroxide + Retinol When Used in Different Slots
docs.text:
Error: No crash. The routine builder flagged a conflict between benzoyl peroxide and retinol even when benzoyl peroxide was in the AM routine and retinol was in the PM routine. These two should not conflict when used at different times of day.

Relevant Context The conflict checker was working on a flat set of all ingredients across both AM and PM slots:

# rules.py — original broken version
def check_conflicts(am_products: list, pm_products: list) -> list[str]:
    all_ingredients = set()
    for p in am_products + pm_products:
        all_ingredients.update(p.ingredients)

    conflicts = []
    for rule in CONFLICT_RULES:
        if rule.a in all_ingredients and rule.b in all_ingredients:
            conflicts.append(f"{rule.a} conflicts with {rule.b}")
    return conflicts

# CONFLICT_RULES includes: benzoyl_peroxide + retinol = True
# flat set had both — false positive conflict raised

Key Observation The conflict rules are written for products used at the same time. Benzoyl peroxide and retinol are incompatible together but are commonly recommended in a split AM/PM routine. Checking conflicts on a merged flat set ignores time-of-day context entirely.

Solution Check conflicts per slot, not across both slots combined:

# rules.py — fixed version
def check_conflicts(am_products: list, pm_products: list) -> list[str]:
    conflicts = []
    for slot_products in [am_products, pm_products]:
        slot_ingredients = set()
        for p in slot_products:
            slot_ingredients.update(p.ingredients)
        for rule in CONFLICT_RULES:
            if rule.a in slot_ingredients and rule.b in slot_ingredients:
                conflicts.append(f"{rule.a} conflicts with {rule.b} (same slot)")
    return conflicts

Because Ingredient conflicts occur when two incompatible actives are applied together on the skin. If they are used in separate routines hours apart, the skin has fully absorbed the first before the second is applied, eliminating the interaction.

docs.title: Junk Entries in Product Catalog After Import
docs.text:
Error: No crash. The seeded product catalog contained entries like:

name: "Unnamed: 0"
price: 0
category: null

These showed up in recommendations and in the ingredients browser.

Relevant Context The catalog was imported from a CSV file without any cleaning:

# seed.py — original broken import
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("products.csv")
for _, row in df.iterrows():
    db.add(Product(**row.to_dict()))

The CSV had an unnamed index column (Unnamed: 0), rows with missing prices, and duplicate entries from multiple download passes.

Key Observation pandas preserves the CSV's index column as a data column named Unnamed: 0 when the CSV was saved with the default index. Zero-price and null-category rows were also present from incomplete data entries.

Solution Clean the dataframe before inserting:

# seed.py — fixed import
df = pd.read_csv("products.csv")
df = df.dropna(subset=["name", "price", "category"])
df = df[~df["name"].str.startswith("Unnamed")]
df = df[df["price"] > 0]
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["name"])

for _, row in df.iterrows():
    db.add(Product(**row.to_dict()))

Because dropna removes rows with null values in required fields. The startswith("Unnamed") filter removes pandas index columns. The price > 0 filter removes placeholder rows. drop_duplicates removes products that appeared in multiple download passes.

docs.title: Week 11 : Inflated Validation Accuracy from Duplicate Images
Validation Accuracy at 96% Due to Near-Duplicate Images
docs.text:
Error: No crash. The first training run reported 96% validation accuracy, which was far higher than expected for a 3-class skin type problem. This was suspicious.

Relevant Context The dataset was collected by scraping images from multiple sources. The train/val split was done randomly without checking for duplicates:

# training notebook — original split, no deduplication
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

all_paths = glob("dataset/**/*.jpg", recursive=True)
train_paths, val_paths = train_test_split(all_paths, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
# near-identical images from the same source could end up in both splits

After training, checking the val set manually showed many images that were slightly resized or re-compressed versions of training images.

Key Observation Near-duplicate images in both train and val sets inflate validation accuracy because the model has effectively seen those images during training. The 96% figure was measuring memorisation, not generalisation.

Solution Compute MD5 hashes for every image, deduplicate on hash, then split:

import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

def file_hash(path):
    return hashlib.md5(Path(path).read_bytes()).hexdigest()

# deduplicate
seen = {}
unique_paths = []
for p in all_paths:
    h = file_hash(p)
    if h not in seen:
        seen[h] = p
        unique_paths.append(p)

# now split
train_paths, val_paths = train_test_split(unique_paths, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

After deduplication, validation accuracy dropped to ~71%, which matched the expected range from the Zhang & Ma paper.

Because MD5 catches exact duplicates. Near-duplicates (same image re-saved at different quality) produce different hashes, but the main issue was exact copies from multiple download passes of the same source. The hash dedup removed those cleanly. The 71% figure is the honest baseline for this problem.

docs.title: NameError: train_loader Not Defined on Kaggle Re-Run
docs.text:
Error: 

NameError: name 'train_loader' is not defined

Appeared on Kaggle when clicking "Save and Run All" after adding new cells to the notebook.

Relevant Context Previous experiments had left stale cells in the notebook that defined train_loader in one place and used it in another. When cells were reordered or deleted the reference broke:

# Cell 12 (from an abandoned experiment — later deleted)
train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

# Cell 18 (still in notebook, referencing the deleted cell's variable)
for epoch in range(NUM_EPOCHS):
    for batch in train_loader:   # NameError: train_loader not defined
        ...

Key Observation Kaggle notebooks execute cells in order on "Save and Run All" but interactive sessions keep variables in memory from previous runs. A notebook that works interactively can fail on a clean run if it has stale cells that were only run manually.

Solution Delete all stale cells and do "Restart and Run All" before every commit:

# Clean notebook structure — define train_loader in the same cell as the training loop
train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)
val_loader = DataLoader(val_dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=False)

for epoch in range(NUM_EPOCHS):
    for batch in train_loader:
        ...

Because "Restart and Run All" clears all kernel state and runs every cell from scratch in order. Any undefined variable that only existed in a previous interactive session will cause a NameError, which is exactly what you want to catch before committing.

The Kaggle NameError was caused by stale cells from abandoned experiments — the fix is to always do "Restart and Run All" before committing a notebook version.

docs.title: Week 12 : Class Imbalance in Skin Type Model
Per-Class Accuracy Imbalance — Dry Class at 0.54 F1
docs.text:
Error: No crash. After training with equal class weighting, the per-class F1 scores showed a large gap:

              precision    recall  f1-score
dry              0.61      0.49      0.54
normal           0.68      0.73      0.70
oily             0.84      0.88      0.86

accuracy                             0.74
macro avg        0.71      0.70      0.70
weighted avg     0.73      0.74      0.73

Relevant Context The dataset had unequal class distribution:

dry:    1,240 images
normal: 2,180 images
oily:   3,650 images

The model was trained with standard CrossEntropyLoss and no class weighting:

# training — original, no class weights
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

Key Observation With an unbalanced dataset the loss function is dominated by the majority class (oily). The model learns to predict oily accurately at the expense of dry, because that minimises the unweighted loss most efficiently.

Solution Compute inverse-frequency class weights and pass them to the loss function:

from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_class_weight
import numpy as np

labels = [label for _, label in train_dataset.samples]
weights = compute_class_weight("balanced", classes=np.unique(labels), y=labels)
class_weights = torch.tensor(weights, dtype=torch.float).to(device)

criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=class_weights)

After retraining with balanced weights:

              precision    recall  f1-score
dry              0.69      0.64      0.66
normal           0.70      0.72      0.71
oily             0.80      0.82      0.81

balanced accuracy                    0.712

Because compute_class_weight("balanced") sets each class weight proportional to n_samples / (n_classes * n_samples_for_class). This penalises errors on minority classes more heavily, pushing the model to learn the dry class better rather than ignoring it.

docs.title: Dry/Normal Confusion Persisting After Retraining
docs.text:
Error: No crash. Even after adding class weights, dry and normal were still confused with each other at a rate that could not be improved by further training.

Relevant Context The confusion matrix after balanced retraining:

Predicted:   dry   normal   oily
Actual dry:   64      31       5
Actual norm:  28      73       9
Actual oily:   3      12      85

Dry and normal had a 28-31% mutual confusion rate. Manual review of misclassified images showed many cases where the two labels genuinely looked the same.

Key Observation Human raters agree on dry vs normal only about 70-72% of the time for borderline cases. The model is hitting approximately the same ceiling. This is a data labelling uncertainty problem, not a model architecture problem.

Solution Document the ceiling and handle low-confidence dry/normal predictions in the backend with a referral flag:

# recommendations.py — referral for low confidence skin type
SKIN_TYPE_CONF_THRESHOLD = 0.60

if result.confidence_skin_type < SKIN_TYPE_CONF_THRESHOLD:
    result.referral_needed = True
    result.referral_reason = "skin_type_uncertain"

Because When the fundamental ambiguity is in the training data labels, more training data or a larger model will not help. The honest response is to surface the uncertainty to the user via the referral flag rather than pretending to a confidence the model cannot have.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This week I completed MobileNetV2 skin type model training with class-balanced weights. The per-class F1 for dry improved from 0.54 to 0.66 by using inverse-frequency weighting. The remaining dry/normal confusion is at the human inter-rater ceiling for this problem (~70-72%), so it is documented and handled with a referral flag for predictions below 0.60 confidence rather than treated as a training failure.

docs.title: Week 14 : Analysis Progress Stuck on Step 0 and DemoBanner Not Clearing
AnalysisProgress Stuck on Step 0
docs.text:
Error: No crash. After submitting a photo, the progress bar would jump straight from step 0 to the final step without animating through the intermediate stages.

Relevant Context The original implementation used .then() chaining to advance through steps, but all the state updates were batched by React before the next render:

// AnalysisProgress.jsx — original broken version
const runAnalysis = () => {
  setStep(1);
  fetch("/api/predict", { method: "POST", body: formData })
    .then(() => setStep(2))
    .then(() => setStep(3))
    .then(data => {
      setStep(4);
      setPrediction(data);
    });
};

Key Observation .then() callbacks fire in the same microtask queue flush. React batches the setStep calls and only re-renders once at the end of the batch, so the intermediate step values are never painted. The progress bar jumps from 0 to the final step.

Solution Use async/await with explicit delays between steps so each setStep triggers a separate render:

// AnalysisProgress.jsx — fixed
const sleep = ms => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

const runAnalysis = async () => {
  setStep(1);
  await sleep(400);
  setStep(2);
  const res = await fetch("/api/predict", { method: "POST", body: formData });
  setStep(3);
  await sleep(300);
  const data = await res.json();
  setStep(4);
  setPrediction(data);
};

Because await sleep() yields control back to the browser between each step, allowing React to flush the state update and repaint the progress bar before the next step fires.

docs.title: DemoBanner Persisting After Live Prediction
docs.text:
Error: No crash. After a user ran a real prediction, the demo banner ("You are viewing demo data") continued to show on the results page.

Relevant Context The DemoBanner component reads dataSource.usedMock from the analysis context, but that flag was never reset before a live prediction attempt:

// Upload.jsx — original
const handleSubmit = async () => {
  // dataSource.usedMock was still true from a previous demo session
  const res = await fetch("/api/predict", { method: "POST", body: formData });
  const data = await res.json();
  setDataSource({ usedMock: false, ...data });  // only set after fetch returned
};

If the user had viewed the demo, usedMock was true in the context. The fetch ran and returned real data, but the banner was visible during the entire loading period and sometimes persisted if setDataSource was not called in the right order.

Key Observation usedMock was only cleared after the fetch completed. During the fetch, and in any error path, it stayed true and the banner remained.

Solution Clear usedMock before starting the live fetch:

// Upload.jsx — fixed
const handleSubmit = async () => {
  dataSource.usedMock = false;   // clear before fetch
  const res = await fetch("/api/predict", { method: "POST", body: formData });
  const data = await res.json();
  setDataSource({ usedMock: false, ...data });
};

Because Setting usedMock = false before the fetch ensures the banner disappears immediately when the user submits a real photo, rather than persisting through the loading period.

The progress animation was not working because React batched the state updates — switching to async/await with sleep() calls between steps fixed that. docs.title: Week 15 : Tab Bar Overflow on iPhone SE and TypeError on Ingredients Page
Tab Bar Items Clipped on iPhone SE (375px)
docs.text:
Error: No crash. On an iPhone SE viewport (375px wide), the bottom tab bar clipped the last item — it was partially off-screen. On larger phones it looked fine.

Relevant Context The tab bar had five items, each with a fixed width:

/* components.css — original */
.tab-bar-item {
  width: 80px;
  flex-shrink: 0;
}
/* 5 items × 80px = 400px — overflows 375px viewport */

// Layout.jsx — original tab bar
<nav className="tab-bar">
  <TabItem label="Home" />
  <TabItem label="Upload" />
  <TabItem label="Results" />
  <TabItem label="Routine" />
  <TabItem label="Profile" />
</nav>

Key Observation 5 × 80px = 400px is wider than a 375px viewport. With flex-shrink: 0 the items do not compress, so the last item is pushed off-screen.

Solution Replace the fixed width with flex: 1 so each item shares the available space equally:

/* components.css — fixed */
.tab-bar-item {
  flex: 1;
  min-width: 0;
}

Because flex: 1 distributes the container's width equally among all children regardless of the total pixel count. min-width: 0 prevents the flex children from overflowing their allocated share if the label text is long.

docs.title: TypeError on Ingredients Page When category Is Undefined
docs.text:
Error: 

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toLowerCase')
  at Ingredients.jsx:47:32

The ingredients page crashed when browsing certain products.

Relevant Context The ingredients component called .toLowerCase() on item.category to filter and group products:

// Ingredients.jsx — original broken version
const filtered = ingredients.filter(item =>
  item.category.toLowerCase().includes(searchTerm.toLowerCase())
);

Some products in ingredients.json had no category field, so item.category was undefined.

Key Observation .toLowerCase() on undefined throws a TypeError. The JSON data was inconsistent — most products had a category but some did not.

Solution Use nullish coalescing to fall back to an empty string when category is missing:

// Ingredients.jsx — fixed
const filtered = ingredients.filter(item =>
  (item.category ?? "").toLowerCase().includes(searchTerm.toLowerCase())
);

Because ?? "" returns an empty string when item.category is null or undefined, so .toLowerCase() always has a string to work on. Products with no category just never match the category filter, which is the correct behaviour.

docs.title: Week 16 : Dark Mode Flash of Unstyled Content and Feedback State Lost on Navigation
Flash of Unstyled Content in Dark Mode
docs.text:
Error: No crash. On hard refresh, the page would flash white (light mode) for a fraction of a second before switching to dark mode, even when dark mode was the saved preference.

Relevant Context The dark mode was applied by a useEffect that runs after the component mounts:

// main.jsx — original broken version
function App() {
  useEffect(() => {
    const saved = localStorage.getItem("theme");
    if (saved === "dark") {
      document.documentElement.classList.add("dark");
    }
  }, []);
  ...
}

Key Observation useEffect runs after the first paint. The browser paints the page once with the default (light) styles, then the effect fires and switches to dark mode. This causes a visible flash.

Solution Add an inline <script> in the <head> of index.html that runs synchronously before any CSS or React mounts:

<!-- index.html — fixed -->
<head>
  <script>
    (function () {
      try {
        var theme = localStorage.getItem("theme");
        if (theme === "dark") {
          document.documentElement.classList.add("dark");
        }
      } catch (e) {}
    })();
  </script>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/src/base.css" />
</head>

Because An inline script in <head> is a render-blocking resource — it runs before the browser paints anything. By the time the first pixel is painted, the dark class is already on the <html> element, so there is nothing to flash.

docs.title: Inline Feedback Widget Losing State on Navigation
docs.text:
Error: No crash. When a user typed feedback text, navigated to another tab, and came back, the feedback form was empty. The feedbackSent flag was also reset, so users could submit feedback multiple times.

Relevant Context The feedback state was held in local component state inside Feedback.jsx:

// Feedback.jsx — original
const [feedbackText, setFeedbackText] = useState("");
const [feedbackSent, setFeedbackSent] = useState(false);
// component unmounts when user navigates away — state is destroyed

Key Observation React destroys component state when a component unmounts. Navigation in a single-page app unmounts the results page, which unmounts Feedback.jsx and resets its state.

Solution Lift feedbackText and feedbackSent to AnalysisContext so they survive navigation:

// AnalysisContext.jsx — added feedback state
const [feedbackText, setFeedbackText] = useState("");
const [feedbackSent, setFeedbackSent] = useState(false);

// Feedback.jsx — now reads from context
const { feedbackText, setFeedbackText, feedbackSent, setFeedbackSent } = useAnalysis();

Because AnalysisContext is mounted at the app root and lives for the full session. State in the context persists across route changes, so the feedback text and sent flag survive navigation between tabs.

docs.title: Week 8 : Confidence Display NaN and Stale Recommendations on Load
Confidence Value Showing NaN% in Results
docs.text:
Error: No crash. The results page displayed NaN% for the confidence score instead of a percentage.

Relevant Context The backend returns confidence as a float between 0 and 1:

{
  "acne_severity": "mild",
  "confidence": { "acne": 0.87, "skin_type": 0.71 }
}

The frontend component was trying to multiply it as if it were already a percentage:

// Results.jsx — original broken version
<span>{Math.round(result.confidence.acne * 100)}%</span>
// result.confidence.acne was undefined because the key was accessed wrongly
// Math.round(undefined * 100) = NaN

Key Observation The component accessed result.confidence.acne but result.confidence could be undefined if the response had not fully populated yet, and the key name used in the component did not exactly match the backend response shape. Math.round(undefined * 100) produces NaN.

Solution Use nullish coalescing to guard against undefined before multiplying:

// Results.jsx — fixed
<span>{Math.round((result.confidence?.acne ?? 0) * 100)}%</span>

Because ?. prevents a TypeError if confidence is undefined, and ?? 0 falls back to 0 so the math produces a valid number. The result displays as 0% rather than NaN% while the data is loading.

docs.title: Stale Recommendations Showing While Fetching New Ones
docs.text:
Error: No crash. When the user navigated to the recommendations page, the previous session's recommendations were visible for a moment before the new ones loaded. There was no loading indicator.

Relevant Context The recommendations component fetched on mount but had no loading state:

// Recommendations.jsx — original
const [recommendations, setRecommendations] = useState([]);

useEffect(() => {
  fetch("/api/recommendations")
    .then(res => res.json())
    .then(data => setRecommendations(data));
}, []);

// rendered the stale cached value from the previous render immediately

Key Observation React initialises state from the previous render's value when the component remounts. The old recommendations were shown until the fetch completed. With no loading indicator the user could not tell if what they were seeing was current.

Solution Add a loading state and clear recommendations before each fetch:

// Recommendations.jsx — fixed
const [recommendations, setRecommendations] = useState([]);
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

useEffect(() => {
  setLoading(true);
  fetch("/api/recommendations")
    .then(res => res.json())
    .then(data => setRecommendations(data))
    .finally(() => setLoading(false));
}, []);

if (loading) return <Spinner />;

Because Setting loading: true at the start of each fetch prevents the stale data from being visible during the in-flight period. .finally() ensures the spinner is removed whether the request succeeds or fails.
